clue.text: They are needed to be a surgeon, or a race-car driver?

definitions.text: They are needed to be a surgeon, or a race-car driver?

parts.words: They are needed to be a surgeon
parts.note: surface reading: the delicate hand control an operating surgeon depends on
setter's reading: a driver needs skill with a fine engine, so the same phrase splits into a quality motor plus driving skills

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the pun: the phrase names precise small movements of the hands, but read as a fine motor plus skills it suits a racing driver too.
explanation.definitionFit: Precise, small muscle movements of the fingers and hands are what a surgeon must have; the phrase is the standard term for them.

clue.text: Take a chance, cooking pilaf with mint

indicators.note: cooking turns raw ingredients into something rearranged

parts.note: to mint is to make money, so a coin is what a mint produces

explanation.surface: A cook gambles by making rice pilaf with mint.
explanation.walkthrough: Mint looks like the herb that flavours the pilaf, but it is the money sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Tossing a coin leaves a decision to luck, the idiomatic picture of taking a gamble.

clue.text: Denies source of nuclear energy before tech tycoon

indicators.note: before places the earlier parts ahead of the tycoon in the down entry
the source of a word is where it starts, its opening letter

parts.note: E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A tech billionaire is denied nuclear power for his projects.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Source of nuclear energy' reads as one idea, a reactor, but it splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To negate a claim is to contradict or deny it, a synonym in the third person.

clue.text: Re: a million bucks for petroleum product

indicators.note: a horse that bucks throws everything into disorder

explanation.surface: A memo headed 'Re: a million dollars for oil'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A million bucks' looks like a sum of money; bucks is a verb, the shuffle signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Mineral oil is a colourless oil refined from crude petroleum, used as a laxative and lubricant.

clue.text: Jam that is set back outside

indicators.note: outside puts the turned word on either side of the other piece
set back means the word for set is turned to run the other way

parts.note: to set something down is to place it
i.e. abbreviates the Latin id est, that is

explanation.surface: A preserve that has gone back to setting on the outside.
explanation.walkthrough: Jam looks like the fruit preserve, and 'set' fits that kitchen picture, but jam here is a blockage.
explanation.definitionFit: A tie-up is a stoppage of traffic or business, a jam in the congestion sense.

clue.text: Hooligans in wild surf taking up one who's wet behind the ears

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the piece is read from bottom to top
taking means holding another piece inside
wild letters run free of their printed order

parts.words: one who's wet behind the ears

explanation.surface: Thugs in rough surf pick up a novice surfer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wet behind the ears' is the idiom for inexperienced, so the piece is a word for a naive beginner; up turns it round inside the shuffled surf.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruffians are violent, lawless people, the same rough sort as hooligans.

clue.text: Plutocrat's soft drink, according to reports

indicators.note: reports are what people say, so the word is judged by its sound

parts.note: the cola brand, said out loud

explanation.surface: A billionaire's favourite fizzy drink, so the gossip says.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles and David Koch were billionaire industrialists famous for funding conservative politics.
explanation.definitionFit: The Koch brothers are a byword for super-rich political donors, so the surname stands for a plutocrat.

clue.text: Lounging and becoming hysterical online?

definitions.meaning: second meaning, punning: typing the internet abbreviation for laughing out loud again and again

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the invented second sense: the online laughing abbreviation turned into a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Lolling means lying or leaning lazily, and read as LOL-ing it means posting that one laughs hysterically.

clue.text: Literary fingerprint found in trusty lexicon

indicators.note: found in says the letters are already sitting inside the words that follow

parts.note: spans the end of trusty and the start of lexicon

explanation.surface: A writer's tell-tale mark is spotted in a reliable dictionary.
explanation.definitionFit: A writer's distinctive manner identifies them as surely as a fingerprint identifies a person, a fresh metaphor.

clue.text: Unsophisticated woman rebuilt engine around the middle of January

indicators.note: around says the reworked letters go on either side of another piece
something rebuilt has had its parts taken apart and put together in a new arrangement
the middle of a seven-letter word is its single central letter, the fourth

parts.note: the fourth of the month's seven letters

explanation.surface: A naive woman overhauls a car engine in midwinter.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged engine letters INGENE wrap around U, giving INGENUE.
explanation.definitionFit: An ingenue is an innocent, artless young woman, especially the stock role of one in a play.

clue.text: Leadership of college taken in by inadequate teachers

indicators.note: a thing taken in by another is absorbed into its middle
the leadership of a word is whatever stands at its head, its opening letter

explanation.surface: A college's leaders are swallowed up by a weak teaching staff.
explanation.walkthrough: C goes inside FAULTY after its second letter, giving FACULTY.
explanation.definitionFit: In American usage the faculty is the whole teaching staff of a school or university.

clue.text: A job for a mechanic and a nanny: getting ripped

indicators.note: the nanny is getting, that is receiving, something inside her

parts.note: an au pair is a young foreigner who lives with a family and minds the children

explanation.surface: A garage worker and a childminder are both working out at the gym.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ripped' looks like slang for muscular, but it is simply the past tense of tear. An au pair is a live-in foreign helper who minds children.
explanation.definitionFit: Fixing cars is exactly the work a garage mechanic does, so this trade name describes the job.

clue.text: Pleasant French city

definitions.meaning: second meaning: the resort city on the Riviera

explanation.walkthrough: The two senses are pronounced differently, which helps hide the shared spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: The everyday adjective for agreeable is spelt the same as the Mediterranean resort on the Côte d'Azur.

clue.text: Preachy claim: "Riots could be chaotic"

indicators.note: anything chaotic is in disorder, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A sanctimonious warning that unrest would bring disorder.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make 'Riots' look like part of a quoted warning; it is fodder alongside claim.
explanation.definitionFit: Moralistic describes someone fond of lecturing others on right and wrong, which is sermonising behaviour.

clue.text: Cheap spies entrapped by cheer

indicators.note: something entrapped is caught and held inside whatever traps it

parts.note: the Spanish shout of approval at a bullfight
the National Security Agency, the US signals-intelligence service

explanation.surface: Low-rent secret agents are lured into a trap by applause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheap spies' reads as one phrase about shoddy agents; cheap is the definition, and the cheer is the bullfight shout.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods offered at a reduced price are cheap, an idiomatic sense of the phrase.

clue.text: Arriving late, female relative keeps branch on the shelf

indicators.note: a word that keeps another holds it within itself
late can mean departed or no longer here, so that part is gone from the word

parts.note: a. is the timetable abbreviation for arrives
a large limb of a tree

explanation.surface: A tardy aunt brings a branch with her, though she is an old maid left on the shelf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arriving late' reads as one phrase, but it is A (arriving) that is late, i.e. gone, from AUNT; the remaining UNT then holds BOUGH.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods still sitting on a shop shelf are ones no customer has purchased.

clue.text: A trio of unfinished symphonies, at the outset, embrace a beginning

indicators.note: an unfinished word stops short of its final letter

parts.note: a trio is a group of that many

indicators.note: at the outset points to the very first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Three unfinished symphonies are taken up at the start of a concert season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unfinished symphonies' suggests Schubert, but unfinished trims the trio, while symphonies supplies only its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A threshold is a doorway, and figuratively the point at which something starts, the brink of a new stage.

clue.text: Deranged maniac covering Romeo's shoulders with a certain feather?

indicators.note: deranged literally means put out of order
shoulders sit at the two edges of a body, so the outermost letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of Romeo

explanation.surface: A madman throws a feathered cape over Romeo's shoulders.
explanation.walkthrough: In 'Yankee Doodle' the hero sticks a feather in his cap and calls it macaroni; the question mark flags that one feather.
explanation.definitionFit: The song's Yankee Doodle named his feather after the macaronis, fashionable dandies of 1700s England.

clue.text: A lunatic is crazy about ships

indicators.note: crazy letters are deranged, out of their sensible order

explanation.surface: Someone mad is obsessed with boats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crazy about' looks like one phrase meaning keen on; split it, and 'about ships' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective covers anything concerning sailors, navigation or seagoing vessels.

clue.text: Obscure, corrupt nun accepts $1,000 right away

indicators.note: accepts means taking another piece in
something corrupt has been altered from its proper form

parts.note: K, for kilo, means a thousand dollars

explanation.surface: A crooked, little-known nun takes a thousand-dollar bribe on the spot.
explanation.walkthrough: K for a thousand comes from kilo; Americans write $10K for ten thousand dollars.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone obscure is not famous, unrecognised by the public at large.

clue.text: Goose ranged freely for a look

parts.note: first meaning: a male of the species

indicators.note: letters moving freely are not tied to their printed order

parts.note: second meaning: informal for a glance, as in take a quick one

explanation.surface: A free-range goose wandered about, looking around.
explanation.walkthrough: Two definitions flank an anagram of 'ranged'; all three point to the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: A male goose has its own name, and the same word is American slang for a quick glance.

clue.text: Doctor! I have a tendency, initially, to steer toward…

parts.note: the standard abbreviation of the title

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter of the neighbouring word

explanation.surface: A patient confesses to the doctor an urge to steer toward something.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs on to the next clue, hinting at Magic Johnson driving to the basket.
explanation.definitionFit: To drive at something is to aim or head for it, the idiomatic sense of intending a goal.

clue.text: Audio equipment in front of Mamie Eisenhower

indicators.note: the front of a name is the letter that leads it

parts.note: the opening letter of the First Lady's first name

explanation.surface: Sound gear set up in front of the former First Lady.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mamie Eisenhower' reads as one person, but it splits: M from Mamie and IKE for her husband.
explanation.definitionFit: Mike is the informal short form of microphone, a basic piece of sound equipment.

clue.text: …Johnson's buddy, capturing soldier

indicators.note: capturing means taking prisoner, holding inside

parts.note: American slang for a pal or guy, as in 'Hey, Mac'

explanation.surface: Johnson's friend seizes a soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Johnson's buddy' looks like Boswell, Samuel Johnson's biographer, but 's here means 'is', and Johnson is the basketball star Earvin 'Magic' Johnson.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lakers point guard Earvin Johnson is universally known by the nickname this answer gives.

clue.text: Deaths as heavyweight boxer evens the score

explanation.surface: A champion boxer settles the score with a deadly comeback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heavyweight boxer' looks like one description of Ali, but it splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Fatalities are deaths caused by accidents, war or disaster, a formal plural noun for them.

clue.text: Let it be heard!

indicators.note: to be heard is to be listened to, so the sound counts, not the spelling

explanation.surface: A command to speak up and say it out for all to hear.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition, an instruction to say something so it can be heard, while 'Let' gives the word that sounds the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Speaking audibly, rather than silently or in a whisper, is what saying something this way means.

clue.text: Mark second part of a train

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second
a carriage of a railway train

explanation.surface: A railway carriage leaves its mark on someone for a second.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark looks like a name; it is the definition, a blemish.
explanation.definitionFit: A scar is a lasting mark left on the skin after a wound heals.

clue.text: Comic actor's Oscar on disc

parts.note: Oscar the Grouch is the Sesame Street character who lives in a trash can
a round letter shaped like a disc

explanation.surface: A comedian's Academy Award is recorded on a DVD.
explanation.walkthrough: Oscar looks like the film award, but here it is the grumpy Muppet. Groucho Marx was the wisecracking star of the Marx Brothers films.
explanation.definitionFit: Groucho Marx, with his greasepaint moustache and cigar, is among the most famous film comedians.

clue.text: Taking Monday off in June, perhaps, I get busy

indicators.note: taking something off a word removes it
completes the instruction: the named day's letter comes off

parts.note: June is an example of one
M is the calendar abbreviation for Monday

explanation.surface: Having a Monday off in June, I find I'm swamped anyway.
explanation.walkthrough: EGO is Latin for I, a common crossword stand-in; get only links it to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone constantly active and rushing about is idiomatically described as never stopping.

clue.text: I don't care if its elements are reused — it's recommended against

indicators.note: reused elements are put to work again in a new arrangement, some of them more than once

parts.note: taken as written; its letters are the elements
six of the same phrase's letters, used a second time

explanation.surface: A shrug of indifference about recycling, followed by a warning that it's a bad idea.
explanation.walkthrough: Not a strict anagram: the answer uses only letters from 'I don't care', with six of them (C, N, T, A, I, D) used a second time, which is why the clue says reused.
explanation.definitionFit: Doctors call a drug or treatment contraindicated when a patient's condition makes it inadvisable.
